notes:
I could find verse-by-verse comment for most of Ezekiel 48, but not every verse. My searches and page fetches ran out before I reached the denominational sites (ligonier, gty, desiringgod, seedbed, lcms and others), netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org and the Catholic and Orthodox sites. So the "traditions" section uses older commentators found on studylight and biblehub, plus Guzik (enduringword) and GotQuestions. Two pages I read in full (Ellicott on studylight and Guzik on enduringword) come with their URLs but no inline citation tags.

**The main split over the whole chapter**
The pages divide clearly into two readings:
- **Literal, future kingdom.** Guzik, quoting Feinberg, says this is a real future kingdom on earth. GotQuestions agrees: Ezekiel 40—48 describes a future temple and city central during the thousand-year reign of the Messiah. (https://www.gotquestions.org/the-LORD-is-there.html)
- **Picture of the church.** Ellicott argues the vision should not be taken literally. His reasons: it was seen "in the visions of God"; returning exiles who heard Ezekiel never tried to carry it out; Hebrews rules out a return to animal sacrifices; and the measurements don't fit the real land. He notes that Ephrem Syrus, Theodoret and Jerome all read it symbolically. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html)
- **Feinberg's reply** (quoted by Guzik): this much detail is "inexplicable" if it is all symbolic. Interpreters take the tabernacle instructions literally, so they should take these literally too. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/)

Labelling these writers by church tradition (e.g. Henry, Benson, Gill, Ellicott) is my own identification; the pages don't state it.

**Verse notes**

**v. 1:** Ellicott says each tribe's strip runs across the whole land from east to west. Dan's old land was west of Benjamin, but part of the tribe captured Laish in the far north, so Dan is now the northernmost tribe. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html) Guzik notes that Dan is left out of the 144,000 in Revelation 7, possibly for its early idolatry. Here it is listed first, which he calls a sign of God's grace. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/)

**vv. 1–7:** Guzik points out that no tribe gets land east of the Jordan, where Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh used to live. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/) Ellicott makes three points (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html):
- The order of the tribes follows neither birth order nor their mothers.
- Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh and Ephraim stay roughly near their old areas.
- Each tribe gets less than two-thirds of what Joshua gave it.

Kingcomments says the northern tribes are listed from north to south. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/ezekiel/48.htm)

**v. 7:** Feinberg (quoted by Guzik) says Judah and Benjamin, the tribes loyal to David's line, are honoured by being placed next to the centre. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/)

**v. 8:** Ellicott explains that the "set-apart portion" (the oblation, already introduced in Ezekiel 45) is described more exactly here. It is 25,000 wide, with its length simply "as one of the other parts", ignoring how the land actually narrows. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html)

**v. 9:** Ellicott says the word "oblation" is used three ways in this passage: the whole strip, the priests' and Levites' part, and the most holy priests' part. The priests' part is named first because it is the most sacred. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html) Clarke places the temple at its centre. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-48.html)

**v. 10:** Ellicott says "in the center" should be taken strictly: the sanctuary sits at the very middle. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html) Guzik says the land is set apart to the LORD, who then gives it to His priests. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/)

**v. 11:** Ellicott thinks the Levites were more caught up in the nation's apostasy than the priests. As evidence he notes that fewer than 400 Levites returned from exile, against 4,289 priests (Ezra 2). (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html) Kingcomments: They are given this excellent place because of their outstanding faithfulness to the LORD at a time when the entire people, including the Levites, have strayed away from Him. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/ezekiel/48.htm)

**v. 12:** Kingcomments says the priests are given charge of this "most holy" land, and their territory borders the territory of the Levites. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/ezekiel/48.htm)

**v. 13:** Bordering the area of the priests will be land God has set aside for the Levites, who would serve at the temple to support and assist the work of the priests. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-48.cfm) Ellicott notes the Levites' land is the same size as the priests'. Under the law, by contrast, they had about three times as many cities. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html)

**v. 14:** Ellicott says the Mosaic ban on selling Levite fields (Leviticus 25:34) is extended here to all their land, because it is "first-fruits". (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html) Kingcomments says the Levites must remain well aware that their land is "holy to the LORD", which means that they may enjoy only its usufruct, meaning they may use it but never own it outright. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/ezekiel/48.htm)

**v. 15:** Ellicott says this leftover strip is called "profane" (common) only in contrast with the holy land of the Levites and priests. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html) Matthew Henry agrees the city was holy, but, in comparison with the sanctuary, it was a profane place. He adds a warning: great cities, even those which, like this, have the sanctuary near them, are profane places. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_048.cfm)

**vv. 16–17:** Wright, quoted by Guzik, says the city is about a mile and a half square, with open land all round. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/) Ellicott notes the city is an exact square. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html)

**vv. 18–19:** Guzik says the farms and gardens there feed the city's people and workers. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/) Kingcomments: the city does not belong specifically to any tribe, but belongs to all the tribes. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/ezekiel/48.htm)

**v. 20:** Bridgeway says The entire portion of land for priests, Levites and national capital was square in plan. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/48-29.html)

**vv. 21–22:** Guzik takes "the prince" to be the ruler the Messiah appoints, as in Ezekiel 45:7–8. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/) Clarke says the prince's land lies east and west of the holy district, with Judah to the north and Benjamin to the south. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-48.html)

**vv. 23–27:** Kingcomments says the five southern tribes also get full-width strips, listed north to south. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/ezekiel/48.htm) Ellicott sees a pattern: the two eldest, Reuben and Simeon, sit next to Judah and Benjamin. He also says Zebulun's and Gad's land would be fit only for nomads unless the land itself changed. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html)

**v. 28:** I found no specific comment on Gad's southern border.

**v. 29:**
- Guzik: Each of the tribes would be restored to the land and none of them will be forgotten before God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/)
- Gill reads the inheritance spiritually. It is not of a worldly, but spiritual nature: a place in God's church and its ordinances. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/48-29.htm)
- The same page argues there will be no need for cities of refuge, because no one will harm or destroy in God's holy mountain (Isaiah 11:9). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/48-29.htm)
- Ellicott sees the loss of cities of refuge as a deep change to the Mosaic law, and another sign the vision is ideal rather than literal. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html)

**v. 30:** Clarke: the Jews would picture their land divided to the twelve tribes, in lots of a regular and mathematical form; and not confused or intermixed, as in Joshua's time. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezekiel-48.html)

**vv. 31–34:** On the twelve gates:
- Block (quoted by Guzik) calls them "strikingly unconventional", since city walls usually had one gate. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/)
- Feinberg sees the end of the old tribal rivalries. (same page)
- Taylor compares Revelation 21, whose gates also bear the tribes' names, with the apostles' names on its foundations. (same page)
- The Homiletical Commentary: The twelves gates bear the names of the twelve tribes, to imply that all are regarded as having an interest in it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-48.html)
- **v. 32:** Guzik notes that Joseph has one gate here, not two. The gates follow Jacob's twelve sons, so Levi has a gate (v. 31). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/)

**v. 35:** The city's size and name.
- **Size:** The whole circumference of the city was 18,000 cubits, or some-what under six miles. Josephus put the Jerusalem of his day at about four miles. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/48-35.htm) Guzik takes the exact measurement as a sign the city is literal. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/)
- **God returns for good:** Guzik says Jerusalem is never named in chapters 40–48 because God gives it a new name. Ezekiel saw God's glory leave the temple (ch. 11) and come back (43:5); now he is assured it will stay. Guzik quotes Spurgeon: the glory of the millennial age is that the Lord is there. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-48/)
- **Future kingdom reading:** GotQuestions: The city Ezekiel saw will rightfully be called Yahweh-shammah, because the Messiah will be there. (https://www.gotquestions.org/the-LORD-is-there.html)
- **Church reading:**
  - Matthew Henry gives three layers of meaning: God present with the returned exiles, with the gospel church by His Spirit, and in heaven. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_048.cfm)
  - Benson gives the same three layers. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/ezekiel-48.html)
  - Ellicott says the vision pictures the glories of the Church of the future. Its high point is the believer living in Christ and Christ in the believer (John 6:56). (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-48.html)
  - Trapp calls it the true Church's name, and the true Christian's happiness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/ezekiel-48.html)
- **Barnes:** Barnes cites Jerome, the early Latin church father: the city is no longer "Jerusalem" but "The Lord is there", because God will never again leave it. Barnes sees the vision fulfilled in Emmanuel, who tabernacled among men John 1:14. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/48-35.htm)
- **Gill:** Gill notes some Jewish writers took the city as the Jerusalem above, in the age to come. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/48-35.htm)
- **Applying the name:** The Biblical Illustrator extends it to cities and the wider social world today. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ezekiel-48.html)

**Not found:** Catholic and Orthodox sources were not reached; Jerome comes only secondhand, through Barnes. I also found no netbible notes, no bibleodyssey material, and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
